Where it began

Arjuna Ranatunga's story starts in Gampaha, near Colombo, where he was born on 1 December 1963. He went to Ananda College and was named the Observer Schoolboy Cricketer of the Year in both 1980 and 1982. Nobody had won it twice before. In 1980 he also played for Sri Lanka's under-20 side against India and made 128 not out in his very first game.

Cricket ran in the family. Two of his brothers, Dammika and Sanjeeva, went on to play Tests for Sri Lanka, and both made their debuts with Arjuna as their captain.

The player

He was 18 when Sri Lanka played their first ever Test, against England at the P. Sara Oval on 17 February 1982. He made 50, the first Test fifty by a Sri Lankan. In June 2000 he played in Sri Lanka's 100th Test too, the only man to appear in both their first and their hundredth.

Against Pakistan at the same ground in 1986, he and Asanka Gurusinha batted through an entire final day without losing a wicket, putting on 240 unbroken to save the match. His share was 135 not out, his best in Tests. In all he played 93 Tests from 1982 to 2000 and made 5,105 runs at 35.70, with four hundreds and 38 fifties.

What made him special

Above all, he was a leader. He took charge of Sri Lanka in 1988 and held the job for eleven years, turning a side that often lost into one that expected to compete. He captained them in 56 Tests and in 1998 led them to their first Test win in England, by ten wickets. In one-day cricket he backed his batsmen to attack hard in the opening overs, when the field was up, and other teams soon copied the idea. It all came together at the 1996 World Cup. Sri Lanka won it, and Ranatunga hit the winning runs in the final, finishing on 47 not out. Across the tournament he averaged 120.50, the best of anyone.

His bowling was a gentler business. His medium pace brought him 16 Test wickets at 65 apiece, so every one of them was well earned. The best of them came in a spell of 2 for 17 against New Zealand at Kandy in the 1983–1984 season.

Away from the middle

In 1999 Wisden named him one of its five Cricketers of the Year. After he stopped playing in 2001 he worked as a television commentator, joined the ICC's cricket committee in 2005 and served Sri Lanka Cricket in several roles, including as its chairman in 2008. He also gave his time to young players, encouraging the likes of Praveen Jayawickrama to take the game seriously. Outside cricket he served for many years in Sri Lanka's parliament, including as a government minister.

And finally

He was there at the very start, a teenager in Sri Lanka's first Test. Fourteen years later he was holding the World Cup. Few cricketers get to see a whole team's story from the opening page to one of its happiest chapters, and fewer write so much of it themselves.
